subject: obstetrics-gynaecology
title: Male Infertility, Semen Analysis and Tubal Pathology

steps.tx: Evaluation of the infertile couple begins with concurrent assessment of **male factor infertility**, contributing to approximately forty to fifty percent of all childbearing delays. Diagnostic evaluation requires a detailed history of testicular trauma, mumps orchitis, cryptorchidism, heat exposure, gonadotoxic medications, and a comprehensive physical examination assessing testicular volume and secondary sexual characteristics.
steps.say: Male factor contributes to half of all infertility cases and mandates simultaneous initial assessment.

vis.caption: Etiologies of male infertility including varicocele, obstruction, and testicular failure. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The cornerstone diagnostic laboratory investigation is standardized **WHO semen analysis**, performed after two to seven days of sexual abstinence. Modern sixth edition World Health Organization reference limits define lower fifth percentile thresholds: semen volume of 1.4 milliliters, sperm concentration of sixteen million per milliliter, and total motility of forty-two percent.
steps.say: WHO guidelines define normal lower reference limits for volume, sperm concentration, and motility.

steps.tx: Strict evaluation of cellular contours using **Kruger strict morphology** requires that at least four percent of spermatozoa exhibit perfect head, neck, and tail parameters. Sperm morphology below four percent, designated teratozoospermia, reflects impaired acrosomal cap formation, defective zona pellucida binding, and impaired fertilization capacity, often requiring intracytoplasmic sperm injection.
steps.say: Strict morphology thresholds identify teratozoospermia and guide the need for assisted fertilisation.

left.title: Normal Sperm Criteria
points: Acrosome covers 40 to 70 percent of head
Straight slender midpiece and uniform tail

steps.tx: A semen analysis report records volume, concentration, motility and shape. **Kruger strict morphology** counts a spermatozoon as normal only when head, neck and tail are all perfect, and at least four percent must meet that bar. Below four percent is teratozoospermia, with poor acrosome formation and weak zona binding, so fertilisation often needs intracytoplasmic sperm injection. When no sperm appear, FSH and testicular volume separate obstruction from primary testicular failure.

vis.caption: The report pairs semen parameters, including strict morphology, with FSH and testicular volume for the azoospermia workup. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The complete absence of spermatozoa from the centrifuged ejaculate pellet defines **clinical azoospermia**. Diagnostic workup requires distinguishing obstructive from non-obstructive etiologies by measuring serum follicle-stimulating hormone and assessing testicular size. Obstructive cases feature normal testicular volume and normal serum FSH, while non-obstructive testicular failure exhibits elevated FSH and small soft testes.
steps.say: Azoospermia is divided into obstructive and non-obstructive types based on FSH and testicular volume.

vis.alt: Diagram of male reproductive tract and vas deferens occlusion.
vis.caption: Anatomical pathways of the male reproductive tract and vas deferens obstruction. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: A common genetic etiology of obstructive azoospermia is **congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens**, found in over ninety-five percent of men with cystic fibrosis. Mutations in the CFTR gene cause failure of mesonephric duct development. Genetic testing of both partners is mandatory before performing surgical sperm aspiration and intracytoplasmic sperm injection.
steps.say: Bilateral absence of the vas deferens is linked to CFTR mutations and requires genetic counselling.

left.title: CFTR Pathophysiology
points: Absent vas deferens and seminal vesicles

steps.tx: Non-obstructive testicular failure frequently arises from the chromosomal anomaly **Klinefelter syndrome**, sporting a 47,XXY karyotype. Patients present with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, small firm atrophic testes, gynecomastia, tall eunuchoid proportions, and azoospermia. Microdissection testicular sperm extraction recovers focal islands of spermatogenesis in approximately fifty percent of cases.
steps.say: Klinefelter syndrome presents with small firm testes, elevated gonadotropins, and non-obstructive azoospermia.

rows: Loss of inhibin B and testosterone feedback

steps.tx: Accounting for thirty percent of all female subfertility cases, **tubal factor infertility** represents mechanical hindrance to ovum pickup and gamete transport. The primary cause is previous pelvic inflammatory disease, with Chlamydia trachomatis causing silent insidious salpingitis, mucosal deciliation, and intraluminal fimbrial agglutination resulting in hydrosalpinx formation.
steps.say: Pelvic inflammatory disease from Chlamydia is the leading cause of tubal occlusive infertility.

steps.tx: The presence of a fluid-distended fallopian tube, termed **hydrosalpinx**, severely impairs natural conception and reduces in vitro fertilization implantation rates by half. Toxic retrograde leakage of hydrosalpinx fluid into the uterine cavity exerts direct embryotoxic effects and impairs endometrial receptivity. Laparoscopic salpingectomy or proximal tubal clipping prior to IVF restores standard implantation success.
steps.say: Hydrosalpinx fluid leaks retrogradely into the uterus, halving IVF success until the tube is excised or clipped.
